extracted.intended_audience: princes, rulers, and political leaders (readers of statecraft and political strategy)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for a prince on acquiring and maintaining power: military preparations, alliances, administration of servants and counsellors, popular policy, and how to manage fortune and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on internal factions
rubrics_metrics.description: Fostering factions among tributary towns (e.g., Guelph and Ghibelline disputes) is an old practice but is unreliable: factions divide cities and, in wartime, the weakest party often sides with outside forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factions may be useful in times of peace to distract citizens, but they are a sign of weakness in a vigorous principality and become fallacious when war comes; the prince should not depend on dissensions as a method of holding subject cities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain your own loyal armed men
rubrics_metrics.description: Armed men in the state should be your own soldiers rather than independent militias or mercenaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With time render previous local armed men 'soft and effeminate' and arrange matters so that all armed men are loyal to you; a prince must have forces that are personally bound to him rather than to local interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fortresses only when circumstances warrant
rubrics_metrics.description: Building fortresses can be useful or harmful depending on whether a prince fears the people or foreigners more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you fear the people, fortresses are advisable; if you fear foreigners more, fortresses may be counterproductive. The best 'fortress' is not to be hated by the people—fortresses cannot save a prince whom the populace hates, especially if foreigners can assist rebels. Examples: demolitions and razings by Nicolo Vitelli, Guido Ubaldo, Bentivogli demonstrate context-dependent utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer not to be hated by the people
rubrics_metrics.description: Being beloved or at least not hated by the populace is a superior security to physical fortifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even well-defended fortresses will not protect a prince if the people hate him, since foreigners will assist a people that has taken up arms; therefore avoid policies that generate popular hatred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use adversity to build renown when opportune
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortune sometimes brings enemies or designs against a prince to give him the chance to overcome them and gain fame; a wise prince may, in some cases, foment some animosity to have an opportunity to crush it and rise in renown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially for a new prince who has more need to earn renown, manufactured or welcomed challenges can serve as a ladder to greatness—this is context-dependent and potentially risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ and favor formerly hostile men who need to prove loyalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Those distrusted at the beginning of a rule often show more fidelity than those trusted from the start, because they must redeem themselves by deeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men who were hostile but now need the prince's favor can be easier to secure and hold tightly to serve faithfully; however, this varies by individual and requires judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess motives of supporters carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: When supporters favored you because of dislike for the previous government rather than natural affection for you, they will be difficult to keep friendly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh why people supported your acquisition of power; those motivated only by discontent with the former regime will require greater effort and may be unstable allies. It is often easier to make friends of those who were content under the former government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undertake great enterprises and set notable examples to gain esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing makes a prince so esteemed as great enterprises and setting a fine example—public achievements raise reputation and hold subjects' attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained, grand projects (military campaigns, reforms) keep the minds of people occupied and admiring; using religion or other plausible pretexts can help to undertake larger schemes and secure resources for them (example: Ferdinand of Aragon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be decisive: choose sides rather than remain neutral
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince is respected when he is either a true friend or a downright enemy; neutrality often leads to ruin because the conqueror will not trust indecisive friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When powerful neighbours fight, declare yourself for one side; being a willing ally who took arms makes you useful and creates obligations; neutrality leaves you at the mercy of the victor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid allying with someone more powerful for offensive purposes unless necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make alliances with a more powerful state to attack others unless compelled, because victory would place you at the discretion of your ally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unavoidable, favor one side carefully, but recognize the long-term risks of being subordinate to a stronger ally (example: Venetians and France vs Duke of Milan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence: choose the lesser evil among doubtful courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments cannot choose perfectly safe courses; prudence is knowing how to distinguish troubles and to choose the lesser evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoiding one danger often brings another; weigh the character of troubles and take calculated lesser risks as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronize ability, commerce, agriculture, and guilds
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince should honor skilled men, encourage commerce and agriculture, reward those who improve the state, and esteem guilds and bodies of citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer rewards that remove fear of expropriation or excessive taxes, hold festivals and spectacles at suitable seasons, and associate with guilds while maintaining the majesty of rank; these actions promote prosperity and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the majesty of rank while showing courtesy
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince should be courteous and liberal to his subjects and guilds but must never abate the majesty of his office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance approachability and honors with clear maintenance of rank and dignity to preserve authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose secretaries and servants by demonstrated intellect and fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of servants reveals the prince's understanding; servants fall into three classes (those who understand themselves, those who appreciate others' understanding, and those who understand neither).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer servants who can be relied upon—able to comprehend or at least appreciate good counsel; the prime error is choosing incapable or self-interested men (example: Antonio da Venafro praised as Pandolfo Petrucci's servant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure servants prioritize the prince's interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A servant who thinks more of his own interests than of his prince's will never make a good servant and cannot be trusted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test servants by observing whether they seek personal profit in matters concerning the state; those who do should not be trusted with state affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep servants honest by honor, enrichment, and constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure faithful servants, a prince should honor and enrich them, share honours and cares, but make them aware they cannot stand alone to prevent excessive ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance kindness with measures that prevent servants from becoming independent or covetous—many honours or riches should not lead to overreaching; mutual dependence fosters trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid flatterers; structure truthful counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are full of flatterers; the only defence is to let men know that telling the truth does not offend you, while not inviting contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a middle course: choose wise men and grant them liberty to speak the truth only on matters you inquire about; question them and listen patiently. Outside this circle, listen to no one and pursue resolved policies. Make clear that free speech when asked is rewarded; punish those who withhold the truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit counsel on your terms and form your own judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince should take counsel when he wishes, discourage unsolicited advice, and then form his own conclusions after listening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be a constant inquirer but a self-forming judgment-maker; anger should be shown if someone has not told the truth. Good counsel is born of the prince's wisdom, not the reverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-centralize reliance on a single prudent adviser or accept too many counsellors
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince who is not wise will not take good advice unless affairs are entrusted entirely to a single very prudent man (but this is insecure); conversely, too many counsellors yield discordant counsels motivated by their own interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid both extremes: do not give total authority to one man (who may seize power), and do not allow uncontrolled multiplicity of advisers (which prevents united counsel). Keep advisers honest by constraint and the prince's oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain military readiness in peaceful times; do not rely on fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Princes often lose states because they make no provision in quiet times and rely on fortune; only provisions that depend on yourself and your valour are reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare defences, maintain an army in the field when possible, secure the people and nobles; sloth during peace leads to ruin when bad times come.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt conduct to the spirit of the times
rubrics_metrics.description: Success depends on directing actions according to the spirit of the times; what succeeded before may fail if times change, so the prudent prince adapts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two men working differently may both succeed if their methods accord with the times; rigidity can cause the cautious or the impetuous to fail when circumstances shift; flexibility and accommodation to changing conditions are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: When fortune favors audacity, be adventurous rather than merely cautious
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortune favors the adventurous; it is better to be bold because fortune (likened to a woman) yields more to audacity than to cold caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When times and temperament align with daring action, pursue bold enterprises (example: Pope Julius II's impetuous campaigns achieved success where deliberation would not).

rubrics_metrics.name: For national liberation: prepare native forces and innovate militarily
rubrics_metrics.description: To liberate Italy from foreign barbarians, a leader must be provided with his own forces—faithful Italian soldiers commanded and maintained by the prince—and may need to invent military variations that exploit defects in Swiss and Spanish infantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit national martial strengths (personal courage, dexterity) and provide leadership that unites and commands; improvements in arms and tactics confer reputation and make a new prince's enterprise possible. Establish new laws and ordinances as part of founding a renewed order.
